content: 1. In five trials, the method of random allocation was unclear, and the heterogeneity could not be explained due to the absence of subgroup analysis. The inconsistency (I²) was 56%. 2. The evidence profile for the risk of falls, as per the WHO iCOPE guidelines, evaluated the effectiveness of exercise interventions versus control in older adults living in the community. This systematic review was conducted by the WHO team in November 2015. 3. The systematic review by Gillespie et al. (2012, updated in 2015) assessed interventions for preventing falls in older adults living in the community. The publication status indicated no changes to the conclusions. 4. The risk of bias was downgraded due to unclear methods of random allocation in seven trials and unclear allocation concealment in 12 trials. Additionally, outcome assessors were not masked in nine trials, with an inconsistency (I²) of 48%. 5. Allocation concealment was unclear in four trials, leading to a downgrade in the risk of bias. Similarly, unclear procedures for masking outcome assessors and managing incomplete data resulted in further downgrades. 6. Imprecision was noted due to small sample sizes (less than 200 participants) in some trials, leading to a downgrade in evidence quality. 7. Group exercise interventions, including multiple categories of exercise, were compared to control groups in older adults living in the community. Subgroup analyses were conducted based on baseline fall risk. 8. Tai chi group exercise was evaluated against control groups, with subgroup analyses based on baseline fall risk. The evidence suggested that tai chi was more effective in individuals not at high risk of falling. 9. Medication withdrawal or review, particularly psychotropic medication, was compared to control groups. The quality of evidence was low, and the findings favored the experimental intervention. 10. Home safety interventions, including tailored assessments and aids for personal mobility, were evaluated. Moderate-quality evidence suggested these interventions reduced fall rates, particularly when delivered by occupational therapists. 11. Multifactorial interventions, involving assessment and active interventions or referrals, were compared to usual care. Low-quality evidence suggested these interventions reduced fall rates in older adults at risk of falls. 12. Exercise interventions, including multimodal group or individual exercises, were found to reduce fall rates. Moderate-quality evidence supported the effectiveness of these interventions. 13. Tai chi training showed limited moderate-quality evidence for reducing fall risk, with benefits observed in individuals not selected for high fall risk. No effect was seen in those at higher risk. 14. Medication reviews and modifications showed very limited low-quality evidence for reducing fall risk. An educational program for general practitioners on medication review was found to be ineffective. 15. Fall prevention interventions are resource-intensive but are likely to provide health benefits that outweigh the implementation burden. Costs can be reduced through task shifting, family involvement, and group-based delivery. 16. Multifactorial interventions may be challenging to implement due to the need for multiple service providers. However, home-based individual exercise may serve as an alternative. 17. The guideline development group strongly believes that fall prevention recommendations will improve health equity and be valued by healthcare providers, older adults, and their caregivers. 18. The group also believes that their recommendations are feasible to implement in both highand low-resource healthcare settings, drawing on experiences from trials using non-specialized healthcare professionals. 19. Medication review and withdrawal of unnecessary or harmful medications are recommended as part of fall prevention strategies.
